body.text: A hobby starts to sound like a line item somewhere between the pottery-studio membership and the camera that needs its own backpack. It doesn't have to. Most of the ones people stick with begin with one small purchase, or none.
Below are fifteen, each with a ballpark starter cost, the cheapest sensible way in, and a first small step. Treat it as a menu. You only need to order one.
About those prices

Every cost here is a ballpark marked 'typically', and yours will differ with where you live, new versus secondhand, and what's on offer this month. We've left out exact figures on purpose because they go stale fast. Online prices also often leave out shipping and tax.

Two habits keep costs down whatever you pick. Borrow first, since many libraries lend more than books and a friend may own a hoop or a spare set of paints. And check secondhand: charity shops, swaps and neighborhood groups are full of barely used supplies.
Make-something hobbies

body.title: Watercolor painting
body.note: A small pan set, one decent brush and a pad of paper will do. Hold off on fancy paper until you've filled a dozen pages with practice.
body.first: Paint a wash in three colors and let them bleed into each other.

body.title: Junk journaling
body.note: A plain notebook, a glue stick and the things you'd normally recycle. The [beginner's guide](/journal/how-to-start-junk-journaling) walks through the first page.
body.first: Glue in one receipt and one ticket, then add a sentence about the day.

body.title: Air-dry clay
body.note: One block of clay and a few acrylic paints will see you through several small projects. No kiln, no special tools.
body.first: Pinch a small trinket dish and leave it to dry overnight.

body.title: Paint by numbers
body.note: The kit includes everything and spares you the blank-page wobble. Choose a small size over a giant canvas.
body.first: Fill in every shape marked with the same number.

body.title: Embroidery
body.note: Beginner kits usually bundle a hoop, fabric, floss and a needle. Learn three stitches (running, back, satin) and you can make plenty.
body.first: Stitch the first outline of the pattern.

body.title: Friendship bracelets
body.note: A few skeins of embroidery floss and a safety pin to hold your work in place. Make one for yourself before you start on gifts.
body.first: Learn the forward knot and make a short striped band.

body.text: Cozy-at-home hobbies

body.title: Jigsaw puzzles
body.note: Secondhand puzzles are everywhere. Check the pieces are all there before you pay, or swap with a friend.
body.first: Sort the edge pieces and build the frame.

body.title: Reading
body.note: A library membership is the best-value hobby upgrade going. A cheap clip-on light makes it cozier still.
body.first: Borrow three books and read the first twenty pages of each.

body.title: Baking
body.note: You probably own most of what a simple batch of cookies or banana bread needs. A mixing bowl and a tray are enough.
body.cost: Groceries you'd buy anyway, or typically under $25 for basics
body.first: Bake a one-bowl recipe and give half away.

body.title: Indoor gardening
body.note: A cutting from a friend's plant in a jar of water costs nothing. Add a small pot and compost when it grows roots.
body.first: Take a cutting, put it by a bright window and check it weekly.

body.title: Creative writing
body.note: A notebook and a pen. Ten minutes on anything at all: a memory, a stranger on the bus, tonight's dinner.
body.first: Set a ten-minute timer and write without editing.

body.text: Out-and-about hobbies

body.title: Birdwatching
body.note: Your eyes, a window or a park bench, and a free bird-ID app. Binoculars are a nice later upgrade, not a ticket in.
body.first: Sit for fifteen minutes and note every bird you see.

body.title: Outdoor sketching
body.note: A pencil and a small sketchbook. Draw a tree, a bench or your coffee cup. The fancy pencils can wait.
body.first: Draw one object for ten minutes without looking at the paper.

body.title: Hiking and local walks
body.note: Comfortable shoes, water and a trail near you. Many public trails are free, though some parks charge for parking or entry.
body.first: Walk a short trail with a friend and turn back at the halfway point.

body.title: Thrifting
body.note: Set a spending cap before you leave, a number you're happy to part with. Look for one thing you'd never buy new.
body.first: Visit one secondhand shop, choose one item and go home.

body.text: Before you buy anything

Walk around your home first. Most starter lists are shorter than they look: a notebook, pens, scissors, a glue stick, a mixing bowl, a baking tray, old jars, comfortable shoes and a tote are probably already here. For the craft hobbies, the one thing worth buying is a small kit or set in the smallest size, so everything arrives in a box. Better paper, a nicer brush, binoculars and a trail-ready daypack can wait until you've done the hobby five times.

Still stuck choosing? Ask what you want from your evenings. Something for your hands: start with the first list. Something quiet: the second. Something that gets you out the door: the third. The [Hobby Finder quiz](/hobby-finder) narrows it down in a couple of minutes.
Four of these can start today for nothing: library reading, birdwatching, a local walk and ten minutes of writing.

body.title: If you want a starter kit
body.dek: Optional. Start with what you have, then upgrade if a hobby sticks.

body.text: Air-dry clay is pottery without the kiln: soft, forgiving, and it dries on its own on a shelf. Shape something small on Saturday, paint it once it's dry, and you have a dish for your rings. Follow your clay's label for specifics.

One honest note first. Air-dry clay is a decorative material. Do not use air-dry clay pieces for food or drink, even if sealed. It is not waterproof, and it is not for use near flame or heat. Check your clay's label for age warnings and other product notes. Plan on pretty things for shelves, desks and dressers and you won't be disappointed.
What you need

essentials: A block of air-dry clay, a small one is plenty for a lumpy first attempt
A rolling pin, a smooth glass or a straight-sided bottle
A work surface you can wipe down, or baking paper taped flat
A few acrylic paints and a fine brush for decorating
optional: A small set of sculpting tools with wooden handles
A silicone mat or craft mat
A fine sanding sponge for dried edges
A water-based sealer, used as its label directs

body.text: A butter knife and toothpick do much of what sculpting tools do. A jar lid cuts a tidy circle, a fork or button makes texture, and a baking tray holds pieces as they dry. White clay is the easiest to paint over. A mat saves your table, and fine brushes let you paint small things like polka dots without blobbing. Buy tools and a mat after you've made three things and know you'll make a fourth.
Make a trinket dish

A trinket dish is the friendliest first project: flat, shallow and hard to get wrong. Rings by the sink, earrings on a desk, a spare key. The making takes one relaxed evening; drying is where the patience comes in.

body.title: Knead
body.note: Take a golf-ball-sized piece, or a bit larger, and knead until it is warm and smooth.

body.title: Roll
body.note: Roll it to an even thickness all over. Uneven slabs can crack as they dry.

body.title: Cut
body.note: Press a jar lid or small bowl into the slab and cut around it, or freehand a blob you like.

body.title: Smooth
body.note: Dip a fingertip in water and smooth the edges and any seams. A little water goes a long way.

body.title: Curve
body.note: Lift the edges slightly, or press the slab gently into a shallow bowl lined with baking paper.

body.title: Dry
body.note: Leave it somewhere dry and out of direct sun, and flip it after a day so both sides dry evenly. Drying usually takes about two to three days, longer for thick pieces or humid rooms, so check your clay's label. Resist speeding it up with heat; drying too fast or unevenly is a common cause of cracks.

body.text: A realistic schedule: shape on Saturday, flip on Sunday, paint midweek.
Three more things to make

items: **A jewelry holder.** Shape a small dish with a raised lip, or press a few short pegs into a slab to hang rings or hoops. Keep it as a decorative tray for a dresser, not as protection for jewelry.

**Ornaments.** Roll a slab, cut shapes with a cookie cutter and poke a hole with a straw before drying. Press in a leaf, a bit of lace or a stamp for texture. Keep them indoors, since clay is not weatherproof.
**Little figurines.** Start with chunky forms: a rounded mushroom, a small cat, a stack of pebbles. Build from a few balls and coils, and score both surfaces before joining them with a little water.

body.text: Finishing

When the piece is fully dry, sand gently, ideally with a damp sponge or fine paper, in a ventilated space; if a dust mask makes you more comfortable, wear one, and check your clay's safety data sheet. Paint with acrylics, let the color dry, then use a water-based sealer if you want a protected finish, following the label. For a spray sealer, follow the can's ventilation and protective-gear instructions. A sealed piece is still not waterproof, so keep it off the sink edge and away from drinks.
If something goes wrong

items: **It cracked while drying.** Drying too fast or unevenly is the usual cause. Next time dry it slowly, out of direct sun and away from heat.
**The edges look rough.** Smooth them while the clay is still soft with a lightly damp fingertip, and go easy on the water.
**The clay has gone hard in the pack.** Store unused clay in an airtight container between sessions, and do not store clay that has had water added to it.

body.title: Shop your hobby
body.dek: Start with clay and what you own. Add the rest when you know what you reach for.

title: Crochet Your First Thing This Weekend
dek: The hook, the yarn, the three stitches that unlock nearly everything, and a first project you can finish in a weekend.

body.text: One hook, one strand of yarn and three stitches get you a surprising distance. Crochet looks harder than it is, partly because a written pattern reads like code. This guide starts with the stitches, then walks you through a flat square.
Crochet uses a single hook where knitting uses two needles, so there is only one live loop to keep track of. The first row will be wonky. That's normal.
What you need

essentials: One crochet hook, in the size your yarn label suggests
A ball of smooth, medium-weight (worsted) yarn in a light color, cotton or an acrylic blend
A blunt yarn needle for weaving in ends
optional: A few stitch markers, or safety pins, to mark the start of a row
A tote to carry it everywhere
A second hook in a different size to see how the stitches change

body.text: You probably own scissors and a bag already, and a friend may have a spare hook and half a ball of yarn. Light, smooth yarn shows each stitch clearly and unpicks without fuss; dark or fuzzy yarn hides your stitches, so keep it for later. If your hand tires, a hook with a comfortable handle is worth the upgrade.
The three stitches that open the door

body.title: The slip knot and the chain
body.note: Every project starts with a loop on the hook, then a row of chains pulled through one after another. It is the foundation of everything.

body.title: Single crochet
body.note: A short, tight stitch that makes dense fabric, good for dishcloths and bags.

body.title: Double crochet
body.note: A taller, quicker stitch with a looser drape, good for blankets and scarves.

body.text: A heads-up before you follow any pattern: US and UK crochet terms differ, so check which one a pattern uses.
Make a flat square

items: Make a slip knot and slide it onto the hook, snug but not tight.
Chain 20, or about as wide as you want the square. Count as you go.
Skip the first chain next to the hook, then work a single crochet into each chain along the row.
Chain one, turn the work around, and work single crochet into each stitch of the previous row.
Count your stitches at the end of every row. If the number changes, the edges are drifting.
Repeat until it is roughly square, then cut the yarn and pull the tail through the last loop.

body.text: Weave the ends in with the yarn needle. Check the yarn label before washing the finished piece, as care varies by fiber. A single row before dinner is a perfectly good first day, and if your hands ache, shake them out and stop. A relaxed grip also makes more even stitches.
Reading a pattern without panicking

A written pattern looks like code at first glance: ch 20, sc in 2nd ch from hook, turn. It's shorthand, and a pattern should list its abbreviations at the top. Read one line at a time with a finger under the part you are on, and do exactly what it says even when it seems odd. The sense arrives a few rows later.
The yarn label does quiet work too: it lists the weight, the suggested hook and care instructions. Keep a label in your project bag so you can match the yarn when you need more.

Once a flat square feels easy, the natural next steps are a longer rectangle for a scarf, a handful of small squares to join into something bigger, or a simple round coaster. They're the same few stitches in a new arrangement.
Common mistakes and fixes

items: **The edges keep growing or shrinking.** You are gaining or losing stitches at the turn. Count at the end of every row and mark the first stitch of each row.
**It's too tight to work.** Try a hook one size up and hold the yarn more loosely. Everyone grips too hard at first.
**A mistake three rows back.** Pull out the hook and gently unravel to the mistake, which smooth yarn allows. Redoing a row is part of the craft, not a failure.

body.title: Shop your hobby
body.dek: A hook and one plain ball of yarn are enough to start.

body.text: Six stitches cover most of embroidery. Learn them on one small hoop and you can draw a daisy, your initials or a wobbly mug in thread. It's portable, quiet and fits in a tote bag, and mistakes mostly disappear into the texture.
Kit or loose supplies?

A kit bundles a hoop, thread, fabric and a pattern, which takes the guessing out of the first project. Loose supplies let you choose your own colors. If you're unsure, a small kit is a sensible first purchase; if you already own scissors and a scrap of cotton, loose is cheaper.

essentials: A few skeins of cotton embroidery floss in colors you like
Embroidery needles, which have a bigger eye than ordinary sewing needles
A piece of even-weave cotton or linen-blend fabric, bigger than the hoop
optional: A water-soluble pen or a pencil for drawing the design
A thread organizer or a few bobbins
A needle minder, a magnet that keeps your needle from vanishing into the sofa

body.text: You probably own scissors, a pencil and a scrap of plain cotton from an old tea towel or shirt. A good small pair of embroidery scissors is the one upgrade you'll feel every time you stitch.
Six stitches worth learning first

body.title: Running stitch
body.note: In and out along a line. The simplest, and it makes dashes and borders.

body.title: Backstitch
body.note: Go back on yourself to make a solid line. This is your outline stitch for letters and shapes.

body.title: Stem stitch
body.note: A twisted rope of a line, ideal for curved stems and flower outlines.

body.title: Split stitch
body.note: Each stitch splits the one before. It makes a neat line and a good edge for filling.

body.title: Satin stitch
body.note: Rows of straight stitches laid side by side to fill a shape with smooth color. Keep stitches short so they do not snag.

body.title: French knot
body.note: A small raised dot for flower centers and eyes. It takes a couple of tries, so practice on scrap first.

body.text: Your first evening

steps: Stretch the fabric in the hoop and tighten the screw until it is taut like a drum.
Draw a simple shape on it: a leaf, a heart, your initial.
Cut a piece of floss about as long as your arm, and separate out a few of its strands, following the floss label.
Thread the needle and tie a small knot at the end.
Backstitch along the outline, keeping stitches about the same length.
Fill the shape with satin stitch, or add three French knots for a flower.

body.text: When finished, check the floss label for care instructions before washing. Test the pen or transfer method on scrap fabric first, and follow its label.
Keeping it going

Embroidery rewards small sessions: ten minutes while the kettle boils moves a leaf along, and a hoop left on the arm of the sofa tends to get picked up. A little pouch with the needle, a few colors and the scissors means a spare half hour doesn't begin with a search.

Before committing to a full pattern, spend an evening stitching a row of each stitch on a scrap, one beneath the other. It becomes a tiny reference sampler and shows you which stitches your hands enjoy. For a second project, trace a simple outline from something you like. Lettering is a good one, since backstitch alone does the job.
Needles are sharp. Store them in a case or a needle minder, and keep them away from small children and pets.
Common mistakes and fixes

items: **The thread keeps tangling.** The piece is too long, or the thread is twisting. Shorten it, and let the needle dangle from time to time so it untwists.
**The fabric puckers.** Pulling stitches too tight is the usual cause. Let each stitch sit flat, and keep the fabric drum-tight in the hoop.
**The back looks messy.** It does for everyone. Keep the knots small and trim the loose ends.

body.title: Shop your hobby
body.dek: A small kit takes the guessing out of the first hoop.

body.text: Watercolor has a reputation for being fussy, and most of the difficulty is water, not drawing. Learn how paint and water behave and the pictures follow, even if you can't sketch a convincing teapot. A soft blue wash is a nice thing all by itself, so practice already looks pretty.
What you need
Paper matters more than anything else. Thin paper buckles and shows every mistake, so a heavier, textured watercolor paper makes a beginner feel better at it than they are.

essentials: A small pan or tube set of watercolors, student grade is fine
Watercolor paper or a watercolor sketchbook, heavier than ordinary sketch paper
One round brush in a middling size
A jar of water and a cloth or paper towel
A plate or old saucer for mixing
optional: A second, smaller brush for details
Masking tape to hold paper flat
A travel set with a built-in palette

body.text: You probably own a plate for mixing, a jar for water, a hard surface to work on and a hairdryer for impatient moments. A pan set is the least fuss, since you wet it and paint. Pick one small set: if the box turns out to hold far more colors than you need (many do), start with three and ignore the rest, and use the brushes that come with it until you want better ones. A sketchbook of proper watercolor paper keeps all your practice in one place, and a portable set suits a park bench or a café table. If you're going to spend on one thing, make it better paper: it improves every painting more than expensive paint does, and artist-grade paints can wait.

Prices vary by shop and brand. Read labels before you buy: avoid materials with lead, cadmium and other heavy metals. Look for the AP seal from ACMI, which marks products certified non-toxic when used as intended; a CL seal means the product carries health warnings. Wash up after painting, and never point a brush with your mouth.
Four techniques, in the order they help

body.title: Flat wash
body.note: Load the brush, then pull an even stripe of color across dry paper, picking up the bead of pigment at the bottom of each stroke. This is the sky, the table, the background of nearly everything.

body.title: Graded wash
body.note: Start with strong color at the top and add more water as you go down, so it fades to nothing. It is the quickest way to make a sunset look deliberate.

body.title: Wet-on-wet
body.note: Touch color to paper that is already damp and watch it bloom. It is unpredictable and delightful, and perfect for clouds, petals and moody backgrounds.

body.title: Wet-on-dry
body.note: Paint onto fully dry paper for crisp edges. Use it for details once a wash has dried, like leaves on a branch or a window frame.

body.text: Generally, paint light to dark. Leave bare paper where you want a highlight, because getting white back later is hard.
Your first evening

steps: Tape the edges of a sheet to a board or a table if you have masking tape. It helps the paper stay flat.
Wet your paints for a couple of minutes so they soften, and fill your water jar.
Paint a flat wash across the top half of the page, then a graded wash below it.
While it is still damp, drop in a second color and watch what it does.
Let everything dry completely, then add one detail on top with the tip of the brush.
Peel the tape slowly. Put the page somewhere you will see it.

body.text: Three small projects that look better than they should

items: **A sunset gradient** (about 30 minutes). A graded wash from warm yellow into pink and a dusty purple, with a dark strip of hills painted on top once it is dry.
**A wet-on-wet bouquet** (about 40 minutes). Dab blobs of color onto damp paper, then add a few green stems and leaves after it dries. The flowers are just soft shapes.
**A color-swatch card** (about 20 minutes). Paint a grid of small squares, mixing a new shade for each. It is practice, a reference chart and a handsome little card at once.

body.text: Once you're comfortable, pocket a small set on your next walk and paint the same view twice, once quickly and once slowly. Compare the two.
Common mistakes and troubleshooting

items: **The paper has buckled.** Too much water on thin paper. Switch to heavier paper, tape it down, and let it dry flat under a book.
**The colors turned muddy.** Too many colors mixed, or layers painted over damp paint. Mix two colors at most and wait for each layer to dry.
**It looks washed out.** Watercolor dries lighter than it looks wet. Add more pigment and less water next time, and layer a second coat once it is dry.

body.title: Shop your hobby
body.dek: A small set and good paper are plenty to begin.

body.text: If you would like a small ready-made box instead of loose pieces, [Creative Hobby Starter Kits That Are Actually Worth Considering](/journal/creative-hobby-starter-kits-worth-considering) explains what to look for.
